planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Minuet is one of the Agriculture Canada-bred dwarf Weigela hybrids developed for exceptional cold hardiness.

directions: Minuet is a compact, exceptionally cold-hardy Weigela hybrid bred at Agriculture Canada's Morden Research Station, bearing ruby-red buds that open to bicolor flowers combining deep pink outer petals with a pale lilac throat, produced in a heavy flush in late spring with scattered rebloom through summer. Its dwarf, dense habit fits foundation plantings and small borders where full-size Weigela florida cultivars would quickly overgrow the space, and its purple-tinged foliage adds subtle color even out of bloom. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest flowering, and prune immediately after the main spring bloom to shape the plant, since flowers form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Tango Weigela (Dark Purple Foliage Cherry-Red Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the deepest foliage color; another Morden Research Station dwarf Weigela hybrid bred for cold hardiness.

directions: Tango bears deep purple-bronze foliage that holds its rich color through the growing season, setting off a heavy late-spring flush of cherry-red, funnel-shaped flowers that continues sporadically into summer. Like its sibling Minuet, it is a compact, cold-hardy Morden-bred hybrid suited to small borders and foundation plantings, with the dark foliage adding season-long interest beyond the bloom period. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, since both flower production and foliage color intensity fade in shade. Prune right after the main spring bloom flush, since Weigela sets next year's flower buds on the current season's growth soon after flowering finishes.

common_name: Rumba Weigela (Reblooming Wine-Red Weigela with Yellow Throat)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; a third Morden Research Station dwarf Weigela hybrid noted for a longer, more repeat-flowering season than most older Weigela cultivars.

directions: Rumba produces wine-red flowers with a contrasting bright yellow throat, a striking color combination unlike the more common solid-pink or solid-red Weigela cultivars, and it reblooms more reliably through summer than many older selections after the main late-spring flush. Its compact, cold-hardy habit makes it suitable for smaller gardens and mixed borders, and it shares the dependable toughness of the Morden-bred Weigela series. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune immediately after the main spring bloom to encourage the strongest summer rebloom, since flower buds form on new growth produced soon after flowering.

common_name: Bristol Snowflake Weigela (White-Flowered Bristol Series Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the white-flowered sibling of the classic red-flowered 'Bristol Ruby', from the same University of Connecticut breeding program.

directions: Bristol Snowflake is the white-flowered counterpart to the long-popular red 'Bristol Ruby', bred at the University of Connecticut in the same program and sharing its vigorous, upright habit and heavy late-spring bloom. Clean white, funnel-shaped flowers open in dense clusters along arching branches, offering a cooler alternative to the reds and pinks that dominate the genus, with light rebloom possible into summer if conditions are favorable. It grows into a full-sized shrub well suited to the middle or back of a mixed border, screening, or informal hedging, and tolerates a range of soils once established. Grow in full sun for the heaviest bloom, and prune immediately after flowering, since Weigela sets next year's buds on wood produced soon after the spring flush.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Tor is a compact, dense selection of the North American native birchleaf spirea.

directions: Tor is a low, dense, mounding selection of the native birchleaf spirea, bearing flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in early summer above neat, birch-like, toothed foliage that turns strong shades of orange and burgundy in fall, a better display than most Spiraea japonica cultivars offer. Its compact, tidy habit and native ecological value make it a good substitute for the more commonly planted Asian spirea cultivars in a naturalistic or wildlife-friendly border. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates a range of conditions once established and needs only an occasional light shearing after bloom to keep its form neat.

common_name: Froebelii Japanese Spirea (Large Rose-Pink Heat-Tolerant Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Froebelii is an older, larger, heat- and drought-tolerant relative of the popular dwarf 'Anthony Waterer'.

directions: Froebelii bears flat, rose-pink flower clusters in early to midsummer on a somewhat larger, more vigorous plant than dwarf cultivars like 'Anthony Waterer', with reddish new growth that matures to blue-green summer foliage and turns burgundy in fall. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established better than many other spirea selections, making it a reliable choice for exposed or difficult sites. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, and shear off spent flower heads to encourage a lighter summer rebloom. Cut back hard every few years in late winter to renew vigor and control size.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; native to subalpine meadows and streambanks of the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies.

directions: Subalpine spirea is a native shrub of high-elevation meadows, streambanks, and open woods across the Pacific Northwest and northern Rocky Mountains, forming a low, twiggy mound topped in early to midsummer with dense, rounded clusters of small, deep rose-pink flowers that draw butterflies and native bees. Its fine-textured, oval leaves give it a soft, informal texture well suited to naturalistic borders, rock gardens, and native plantings at moderate to higher elevations. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it prefers cooler summers and may struggle in hot, humid lowland climates outside its natural range. Little pruning is needed beyond removing older, woody stems occasionally to keep the colony vigorous.
scientific_name_note: Sometimes treated as a synonym of Spiraea splendens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Douglas spirea spreads by rhizomes and is best sited where a colonizing native wetland shrub is welcome.

directions: Douglas spirea, commonly called hardhack, is a rhizomatous native wetland shrub of the Pacific Northwest and northern California, forming dense thickets in wet meadows, streambanks, and marsh edges. In summer it produces distinctive dense, narrow, spike-like clusters of small pink to rose-purple flowers, quite different from the flat-topped clusters typical of most cultivated spirea, giving it a bottlebrush-like silhouette. It tolerates consistently wet or seasonally flooded soil better than almost any other spirea, making it valuable for rain gardens, pond margins, and streambank stabilization plantings. Grow in moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade, and give it room to spread by suckering rhizomes into a naturalized colony rather than a tightly contained specimen.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; white meadowsweet is a wide-ranging eastern and midwestern native distinct from the already-present hardhack spirea (S. tomentosa), which bears pink rather than white flowers.

directions: White meadowsweet is a wide-ranging native wetland shrub of eastern and midwestern North America, forming upright, narrow clumps of slender, toothed leaves topped in summer with dense, conical spikes of small, creamy-white flowers that draw a wide range of pollinators. It tolerates consistently moist to wet soil, including seasonally flooded ground, making it valuable for rain gardens, wet meadow restorations, and pond or stream margins. Grow in moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; it spreads modestly by rhizome to form a loose colony over time but is less aggressive than the closely related, pink-flowered hardhack (Spiraea tomentosa). Cut back older stems occasionally in late winter to keep the colony vigorous and floriferous.
